messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: knitr 0.3 is ready
parts:
Hi guys,

I planned to release knitr 0.3 one week ago, but baptiste mentioned a
useful new feature (https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/142) which I
really wanted to bring to the new version, so I went ahead and
implemented it. Briefly speaking, this feature means your chunk
options will be parsed as R code instead of a text string, e.g.

<<mychunk, eval=dothis, echo=c(1, 3), fig.cap=paste('the value of pi is', pi)>>=

this gives you full power of options; you can pass anything to chunk
options, and this will greatly extend the power of hooks as well.

I also tried to keep backward compatibility: if your chunk options are
not valid R code, the old way of parsing will still be used. I tested
it on all my manuals, it worked fine with old options, so I guess it
will not bring much trouble to you. More details at:
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/sweave/

Other news at: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS

Before I release the new version to CRAN, I'd like to ask you to test
it to see if there are fatal compatibility issues. I do not want to
see furious knitters jumping over me if this new version breaks their
old documents. Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

There is no package option named 'output':

output path is setwd(wd).

I will update the NEWS file and mention 'output' is an argument of

messages.subject: Re: knitr 0.3 is ready
parts:
Alright, looks like my error.

But let me get this straight: According to ?knit, R code chunks are
executed in the directory where the .Rnw file is located (makes
sense), but the default output location for the .tex file is the
directory where R is currently pointing as given in getwd()? If you
make the default output directory different than the input file
directory then you have to type a lot more, since you have to specify
output each time. For instance, if R was launched in

/Users/bryanhanson

but I want to knit a file in /Users/bryanhanson/Desktop/temp, then I
have to type something like this:

knit("/Users/bryanhanson/Desktop/temp/file.Rnw", output = "/Users/
bryanhanson/Desktop/temp/file.tex")

otherwise the output .tex file goes to /Users/bryanhanson and I have
to go find it and move it. This is made all the more tedious as I may
have changed the current wd using setwd() several times since I last
launched R.

I think this new structure is designed to accommodate those with
really elaborate LaTeX document structures where the parts are spread
around, but it works against the (almost certainly) more common
situation where everything is in one directory, so the typical user is
having to type a lot more.

Unfortunately, I don't think you can't fix this with setwd() inside a
code chunk, because by then knit has already determined where things
will go.

Am I misunderstanding or missing a simple fix? I guess I could do a
setwd() everytime before running knit and then I don't have to specify
anything extra. Either way, keep it up Yihui, it's great! Bryan

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: knitr 0.3 is ready
parts:
Well, what you described is exactly what I have been thinking when I
was developing knitr. In the beginning, I only work with single
documents (no children or parents), so I set the output directory to
be the same as these documents by default. Later, I received more and
more requests about child documents, and I began to feel this was not
a good default. It is much cleaner not to tie input with output.

In the past I did not like setwd() to long directory names either, but
later my practice changed: I always start R (in the terminal) in the
directory in which I want to work, so I do not need to wrestle with
setwd() frequently. In your case, I would do this:

cd ~/Desktop/temp/
R
library(knitr)
knit('file.Rnw')

But you are probably using R.app under Mac, so you have to change the
working directory after you start the GUI. I tend to recommend useRs
to learn this by heart:

Man, know thy getwd()!

-----

If you still find this messy, I have another weapon for you (read the
second paragraph of my reply):
https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=en&fromgroups#!topic/knitr/f9WuyKszW7c

You can call knitr via command line after you added the executable
'knit' to your PATH:

cd ~/Desktop/temp/
knit file.Rnw --pdf

In this case, you do not need to open R at all.

-----

If this still sounds horrible, I bet RStudio should be handy:
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/rstudio/ This boils down to one single
click from Rnw to PDF.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
